children: is open to the idea of upgrading its New York listing to replace the American depositary receipts that currently give its U.S. investors ownership of the Danish drugmaker, The Financial Times reported on Wednesday following an interview with its CEO, Mike Doustdar.

“I clearly do see some advantages with that,” Doustdar, the first foreigner to lead the weight-loss drugmaker, told the FT, adding, “I’m a type who doesn’t start with a 'no' typically; I start with ‘maybe, Can you give me the pros and the cons of that, and let’s have a dialogue and discussions about it?"

Doustdar said that while plans for a direct U.S. listing have been discussed in the past decade, the company is not considering the idea currently. There had been no “active dialogue or discussions” about the topic since he took leadership last year, he added.
Denmark’s largest company by market capitalization, Novo
, is currently listed on Nasdaq Copenhagen even though it generates more than half its revenue from the U.S., the country where a growing percentage of its investor base resides.

“Our investor community, to a larger extent, has shifted over the last 20 years [outside of] Scandinavia, and we are increasingly speaking to investors in the US . . . in addition to [our long-term investors],” Doustdar said.
competed with a direct U.S. listing this year while maintaining its primary listing and headquarters in the U.K. The Anglo-Swedish drugmaker also keeps a listing in Stockholm.

“The U.S. is a strategic country now, has been in the past, and will be in the foreseeable future,” he said, adding Novo
is “a Danish-origin company which is now global and international and operates successfully and proudly across all different corners of the world, and that’s the type of a company I like to lead."
